report:
# Does Offering HIV Self-Testing Increase HIV Testing Uptake?

**Conclusion: Yes.** Randomized controlled trial evidence consistently shows that offering HIV self-testing (HIVST) as an additional option substantially increases the uptake of HIV testing compared to standard testing services alone.

## Evidence Summary

The strongest evidence comes from systematic reviews pooling data across multiple RCTs. A comprehensive review examining HIVST versus standard HIV testing services found that HIVST increased testing uptake overall by more than double (RR: 2.09; 95% CI: 1.69–2.58; p < 0.0001) across 13 RCTs, with moderate-certainty evidence supporting this effect ([thelancet.com/eclinm](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/eclinm/article/PIIS2589-5370(21)00271-6/fulltext)). This 2021 review updated an earlier 2017 analysis that similarly concluded HIVST is associated with increased uptake and frequency of testing across RCTs, particularly benefiting populations at risk who might not otherwise test ([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.7448/IAS.20.1.21594)).

This body of evidence directly informed global health policy: the World Health Organization's 2016 recommendation supporting HIVST was based on trial data showing it as "a safe, accurate and effective way to reach people who may not test otherwise, including people from key populations, men and young people" ([who.int](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/WHO-CDS-HIV-19.36)).

A related synthesis reinforced this pattern, noting that "HIVST doubled the uptake of HIV testing in the general population compared to standard of care," with nearly all trials (12 of 13) supporting this direction of effect ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/am/pii/S2589537021002716)).

## Caveat

While uptake effects are robust, some individual trials—particularly in specific populations like truck drivers in Kenya—found no significant difference, suggesting effect sizes may vary by context and population. Additionally, while uptake increases, some reviews note self-testing may not proportionally increase positive-case yield and can complicate linkage-to-care outcomes—separate issues from the uptake question itself.

**Overall**, the weight of RCT evidence supports that offering HIV self-testing meaningfully increases the number of people who test for HIV.
